data.text/markdown:
Multilingual BPE Tokenizer — a fair, documented walkthrough

This notebook builds one shared 10,000-token BPE tokenizer for the India Wikipedia page in English, Hindi, Telugu, and Maithili, and shows — honestly and step by step — how the design evolved. Assignment score = 1000 / (X4 − X1) where each language's fertility is X_L = tokens(L) / faithful_units(L), and X4/X1 are the largest and smallest of the four. A tighter spread ⇒ a higher score. Hard gates: vocab = 10000, every X_L ≤ 1.2, decode(encode(t)) preserves visible characters, and zero UNK.
Everything below runs from scratch in this kernel. No numbers are hard-coded — each table is computed live.

1 · Import the dataset

Four wiki-faithful Markdown pages, one per language. "Faithful" means the HTML→Markdown conversion keeps links, tables, references, and categories, so the text mirrors what a real page contains.
Loaded characters per language: EN 598,265 · HI 266,728 · TE 113,835 · MAI 17,919

The faithful-unit denominator

The score's denominator counts faithful units: one contiguous run of Unicode letters / combining-marks / numbers is one unit, and each visible non-space punctuation/symbol character is one unit. This is the grader's exact rule, so we use it everywhere.

2 · TokenizerStatsV2 — counting statistics for training

BPE repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent symbol pair. Doing that naively re-scans the whole corpus every merge. TokenizerStatsV2 pre-computes four bookkeeping structures once so every merge is cheap. The four variables it holds (documented):
variable type what it stores why
token_freq Counter[str] how many times each pre-token (word/sentence/line) occurs dedup: identical text is counted once and weighted by frequency
token_to_symbols_map dict[str, list[str]] each pre-token's current symbol sequence updated in place as merges apply — avoids re-symbolizing
pair_freq Counter[(str,str)] frequency of every adjacent symbol pair across the corpus the quantity we maximize each step
pair_to_token_map dict[(str,str), set[str]] inverse index: which pre-tokens contain a given pair so a merge only touches the pre-tokens that actually contain that pair
The dedup in token_freq is what makes this fast: a page has the same words/lines many times, and we process each unique one once.

3 · BPETokenizer — hand-written, no libraries

This tokenizer is written entirely by hand — no tokenizers, no sentencepiece, no tiktoken. Just the standard library. Every merge, the encode path, and the decode path are ours.

3.1 · It began as a subword tokenizer

I first built this to optimize subword tokenization (merges that stay inside a single word, GPT-2 style). I did not yet realize subword-only BPE cannot reach a good score on this metric — Indic scripts stay near ~1.5 tokens/unit and the ≤1.2 gate fails. Later I extended the very same trainer to merge across more than one word (sentences, then whole lines). The training loop below is unchanged between those modes; only the unit we feed it changes.

3.2 · A max-heap, because I like performance

To keep training fast — I like performance — the loop uses a max-heap of pair frequencies instead of re-scanning for the best pair each step. Popping the top pair is O(log n), and after a merge we only push the pairs that actually changed. Combined with the dedup in TokenizerStatsV2, this brings the hand-written trainer close to what a production tokenizer does.

3.3 · Encode / decode

I took help writing the encode and decode methods — greedy rank-ordered merge application on encode, and byte-symbol → UTF-8 reconstruction on decode (lossless by construction).

4 · Train on English, inspect vocab + merges, check round-trip

A quick smoke test on English alone: train a small vocab, look at a sample of the learned tokens and merges, and confirm the round-trip is lossless.

Vocab size: 2,000  •  merges learned: 1,740 Sample learned tokens: ia, wi, ki, wiki, dia, or, en, pe, tt, ](, ps, htt, :/, ://, https, https://, ](https://, in, an, g/ First 15 merges: ('i'+'a'), ('w'+'i'), ('k'+'i'), ('wi'+'ki'), ('d'+'ia'), ('o'+'r'), ('e'+'n'), ('p'+'e'), ('t'+'t'), (']'+'('), ('p'+'s'), ('h'+'tt'), (':'+'/'), (':/'+'/'), ('htt'+'ps') Round-trip probe — India's population is 1,428,627,663. → decode(encode(x)) == x? True ✅

5 · All four languages at once — subword fertility is not good enough

Now train one shared 10k vocab on all four languages at the subword level and score it. This is where I learned subword-only BPE fails: the Indic fertilities sit well above the 1.2 bar.

data.text/markdown:
The score is poor and several languages break X ≤ 1.2. Insight #1: a token can never be shorter than one word if merges are trapped inside words. To get fertility below 1, a token must span multiple words — so let merges cross word boundaries.

6 · Insight: split by sentences to merge across words

The first way to let merges cross words: feed the trainer sentences instead of words. Now a frequent multi-word span inside a sentence can collapse to a single token, pulling fertility below 1.

7 · SentenceBPETokenizer — a child class that merges across a sentence

Exactly like the paragraph tokenizer we settle on later, but the unit is a sentence. The only override is encode: split into sentences and let merges span each sentence. Training reuses the parent loop unchanged.

data.text/markdown:
8 · Round-trip validated, score up — but not enough

Sentence-level clears the ≤1.2 gate and roughly doubles the score. Yet the spread is still wide, because within a single sentence there aren't many repeated multi-word spans to collapse.

9 · Insight: process paragraphs (every new line) for more duplicates

Insight #2: we didn't get enough duplicate spans inside one sentence. If we let a merge span an entire line/paragraph, far more repeated material (list items, table rows, boilerplate) collapses into single tokens. This is the most aggressive cross-word setting.

10 · Scores so far

Paragraph-level with equal weights already lands all four fertilities below 1 — but one lever remains: how the 10k vocab is split across languages (by upsampling each language's lines before pooling). A language given more weight receives more merges and its fertility drops. The final solution tunes those weights to make the four fertilities converge, which is what actually maximizes the score.

11 · The solution we present, and the experiment tables

The champion feeds the trainer paragraphs and upsamples with weights EN:2 HI:2 TE:3 MAI:2, converging all four fertilities into a tight 0.567–0.667 band.
